days.learn: Classes vs records vs structs; nullable reference types; enums
days.title: Domain: Company, JobApplication, Interview and ApplicationStatus
days.doneWhen: `dotnet build -warnaserror` passes with Company, JobApplication, Interview and ApplicationStatus in JobHunt.Domain
days.brief:
### Why this matters
The domain model is the vocabulary of the whole app: every table, endpoint and screen starts here. Choosing between class, record and struct is a classic C# interview topic, and nullable reference types catch null bugs at compile time.

### What you'll build
In `JobHunt.Domain`, on a branch `feature/domain-model`:
- `ApplicationStatus` enum: `Applied`, `Interviewing`, `Offer`, `Rejected`
- `Company` class: `Id` (`Guid`), `Name` (required), `Website?`, `Location?`
- `JobApplication` class: `Id`, `CompanyId` and a `Company` reference, `RoleTitle`, `AppliedOn` (`DateOnly`), `Status`, `SourceUrl?` and a read-only `Interviews` collection
- `Interview` class: `Id`, `JobApplicationId`, `Round`, `ScheduledAt` (`DateTimeOffset`), `Notes?`

### Step by step
1. Create folders `Companies`, `Applications` and `Common`.
2. Write the enum first and decide the starting status for a new application.
3. Write the entities as classes with `private set` properties and constructors taking every required value. Take a `Company` and set both `Company` and `CompanyId`. Ids: `Guid.CreateVersion7()`.
4. Back `Interviews` with a private `List<Interview>` exposed as `IReadOnlyCollection<Interview>`.
5. Mark only truly optional values with `?` and guard required strings in constructors.
6. Run `dotnet build -warnaserror` and fix every nullable warning properly.

```csharp
public sealed class JobApplication
{
    private readonly List<Interview> _interviews = [];
    public Guid Id { get; private set; }
    public IReadOnlyCollection<Interview> Interviews => _interviews;
    // TODO: constructor with guards, other properties
}
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Zero warnings with `-warnaserror`
- [ ] No public setters, and `Interviews` is read-only from outside
- [ ] Domain has no references
- [ ] Names match exactly

### Hints
- `ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(value)` is a one-line guard.
- `DateOnly` fits "applied on"; `DateTimeOffset` fits "interview at 10:00 in a time zone".

### Common mistakes
- Making entities records: two applications with the same data would compare equal.
- Silencing warnings with `null!`.

### Check your understanding
- What does the compiler generate for a `record` that it does not for a `class`?
- When would you pick a `record struct`?
- Nullable reference types are compile-time only. What does that mean for incoming JSON?

days.learn: Mirroring API models in TypeScript: types vs interfaces, union types for statuses
days.title: TS types for Company, JobApplication, Interview and the status union
days.doneWhen: `web/src/types/application.ts` type-checks against a sample `JobApplication`, and every field difference from the C# classes is noted in a comment
days.brief:
### Why this matters
The front end needs its own model of the domain. Mirroring C# types in TypeScript, and knowing where they differ (dates arrive as strings, enums as text), prevents a whole class of runtime bugs. Today's .NET part writes the C# side of the same model.

### What you'll build
In `web/src/types/application.ts`:
- `ApplicationStatus` as a union of string literals: `"Applied" | "Interviewing" | "Offer" | "Rejected"`
- `Company`, `JobApplication` and `Interview` types mirroring the C# entities
- Dates typed as `string` (ISO format), because that is what JSON gives you
- An exported `applicationStatuses` array so the UI can loop over every status

### Step by step
1. Open your C# classes side by side and write each TypeScript type field by field.
2. Decide how optional fields look: `website?: string` (may be missing) or `website: string | null` (always present, maybe null). The API will send `null`, so prefer the second.
3. Decide how an application shows its company name: embed `company: { id; name }` or keep only `companyId`. Pick one and note why.
4. Write `const applicationStatuses = [...] as const` and derive the union from it with `(typeof applicationStatuses)[number]`.
5. Create a `sample` object typed as `JobApplication` in a scratch file and run `npm run build`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No `any`
- [ ] The status union has exactly the four C# values, spelled the same
- [ ] Dates are `string`, not `Date`
- [ ] Optional C# fields are `T | null` in TypeScript

### Hints
- `type` and `interface` both work for object shapes. Pick one convention for models and stay consistent.
- `as const` keeps literal types instead of widening them to `string`.

### Common mistakes
- Typing dates as `Date`. JSON has no date type; you get strings until you convert them.
- Using a TypeScript `enum` by habit. Unions of strings match JSON exactly and add no runtime code.
- Different casing from the API. JSON from ASP.NET Core is camelCase by default.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a `Paged<T>` generic type now; you will need it in week 5.

### Check your understanding
- Why are dates `string` in your TypeScript types?
- What is the difference between `field?: T` and `field: T | null`?
- How does `as const` let you get a union and an array from one source?

days.learn: Guard clauses and domain exceptions; rules inside entities
days.title: Status transitions (Applied → Interviewing → Offer/Rejected) with a domain exception
days.doneWhen: `JobApplication` exposes a method for every legal status change and throws `InvalidStatusTransitionException` for every illegal one

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Exceptions and exception handling
Microsoft Learn: Best practices for exceptions

days.brief:
### Why this matters
If any code can write `application.Status = Offer`, the rules live in whoever remembers them. Putting rules inside the entity means the API, a background job and a test all go through the same check. "Where do your business rules live?" is a favourite design question.

### What you'll build
- Allowed transitions: `Applied` → `Interviewing` or `Rejected`; `Interviewing` → `Offer` or `Rejected`; `Offer` and `Rejected` are final
- Methods on `JobApplication`: `StartInterviewing()`, `ReceiveOffer()`, `Reject()`
- An abstract `DomainException` in `Common` and `InvalidStatusTransitionException` carrying `From` and `To`
- `ScheduleInterview(...)` allowed only while `Applied` or `Interviewing`, moving `Applied` to `Interviewing` automatically

### Step by step
1. Write the transition table on paper, including the illegal moves.
2. Create the two exception classes with a message like "Cannot move from Offer to Interviewing".
3. Add a private helper that checks a move. A `switch` expression on a tuple reads well.
4. Implement each public method: guard first, then set `Status`.
5. Guard `ScheduleInterview` and reuse the helper for the automatic move.
6. Check that no constructor parameter lets callers skip the rules: new applications always start as `Applied`.

```csharp
private static bool IsAllowed(ApplicationStatus from, ApplicationStatus to) => (from, to) switch
{
    (ApplicationStatus.Applied, ApplicationStatus.Interviewing) => true,
    // TODO: the rest
    _ => false
};
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every legal move works through a method
- [ ] Every illegal move throws with `From` and `To` set
- [ ] `Status` cannot be set from outside the class
- [ ] Guards come before any state change

### Hints
- Guard clauses: check, throw, then do the work. No nested `if` pyramids.
- Keep the allowed moves in one place so Wednesday's tests can cover them with one `Theory`.

### Common mistakes
- Changing the status before validating, which leaves a half-updated object.
- Throwing `InvalidOperationException` everywhere. A specific exception lets the API map it to the right status later (week 6).

### Check your understanding
- Why should the rule live in the entity rather than in an endpoint?
- What is the difference between a broken rule and a validation error for bad input?
- How could a caller check a move without catching an exception?

days.learn: Components and props; composing small components
days.title: ApplicationCard component with typed props and a status pill
days.doneWhen: An `ApplicationCard` renders a sample application with a `StatusPill`, and adding a fifth status to the union is a compile error in `StatusPill`

learnLinks.label: react.dev: Passing props to a component

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Small components with typed props are what interviewers look for in live React rounds. Splitting a card into a card plus a pill teaches you when a piece of UI deserves its own component. The pill shows the same four statuses whose rules today's .NET part enforces.

### What you'll build
- `features/applications/ApplicationCard.tsx`: role, company name, applied date and a status pill
- `features/applications/StatusPill.tsx`: a label and CSS class per status
- A `Record<ApplicationStatus, ...>` map so a missing status is a compile error

### Step by step
1. Create `features/applications/` for everything about applications.
2. Write `StatusPill({ status }: { status: ApplicationStatus })` with a `Record` that maps each status to a label and a class name.
3. Write `ApplicationCard` with a props interface that takes one `JobApplication`.
4. Format `appliedOn` with `Intl.DateTimeFormat` or `toLocaleDateString`.
5. Compose: the card renders the pill. Render one card from `HomePage` with sample data.
6. Add `"Withdrawn"` to the union temporarily and read the error, then remove it.

```ts
const statusStyle: Record<ApplicationStatus, { label: string; className: string }> = {
  // TODO: one entry per status
};
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] No `any`; both components have typed props
- [ ] The pill uses a `Record`, not a chain of `if`s
- [ ] The card does no fetching or state
- [ ] Lint and build pass

### Hints
- Keep components presentational: props in, JSX out.
- A small component with one job is easier to test and reuse than a big one with flags.

### Common mistakes
- Passing many loose props (`role`, `company`, `date`...) when one typed object is clearer.
- Building class names with string concatenation from unknown input.
- Calling `new Date(appliedOn)` on a date-only string and getting the day before in some time zones; test it.

### Check your understanding
- When does a piece of JSX deserve its own component?
- How does `Record<K, V>` force you to handle every status?
- What makes a component "presentational"?

days.title: Domain.Tests covering every allowed and forbidden transition
days.doneWhen: `dotnet test` from /api is green and every row of the transition table appears in a `Theory`

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Unit testing C# with xUnit

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Rules without tests are rules you are afraid to change. Domain tests are the fastest tests you will ever write: no database, no HTTP. Interviewers ask about `Fact` vs `Theory` and Arrange-Act-Assert, and a green suite is the first thing a reviewer looks for.

### What you'll build
- `api/tests/JobHunt.Domain.Tests` (xUnit), in the solution and referencing Domain
- `Fact` tests for constructor guards (blank role title, empty company name)
- One `Theory` for every legal transition and one for every illegal transition
- Tests for `ScheduleInterview`: the automatic move and the rejected case

### Step by step
1. From `/api` run `dotnet new xunit -n JobHunt.Domain.Tests -o tests/JobHunt.Domain.Tests`, add it to the solution and reference Domain.
2. Delete the sample test. Name tests by behaviour, for example `Reject_from_Offer_throws`.
3. Write the guard `Fact`s with `Assert.Throws<T>`.
4. Write a small helper that builds an application in a given status through the public methods.
5. Write the legal `Theory`, then the illegal one, asserting the exception type and its `From`/`To`.
6. Run `dotnet test` and make one test fail on purpose to read the output.

```csharp
[Theory]
[InlineData(ApplicationStatus.Offer, ApplicationStatus.Interviewing)]
// TODO: more rows
public void Illegal_transition_throws(ApplicationStatus from, ApplicationStatus to) { /* TODO */ }
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `dotnet test` is green
- [ ] Every legal and illegal move is a `Theory` row
- [ ] Each test follows Arrange-Act-Assert with one reason to fail
- [ ] No test-only setters were added to Domain

### Hints
- `InlineData` takes compile-time constants, so enum values work directly.
- Blank lines between Arrange, Act and Assert make the structure visible without comments.

### Common mistakes
- Many asserts on unrelated things in one test, so a failure does not say what broke.
- Adding public setters just to make testing easier. Reach states through the real methods.

### Check your understanding
- When do you choose a `Theory` over several `Fact`s?
- Why do domain tests not need mocks?
- What makes a test name useful when it fails in CI?

days.learn: Rendering lists with keys; conditional rendering
days.title: ApplicationList rendering sample data, with an empty state
days.doneWhen: `ApplicationList` renders 6 to 8 sample applications with `id` keys and no console key warnings, and shows an empty message for an empty array
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Every app is mostly lists. Keys and conditional rendering look trivial, yet index keys and missing empty states are the two most common review comments on junior React code. The sample data covers the statuses your .NET tests check today.

### What you'll build
- `features/applications/sampleData.ts` with 6 to 8 realistic applications covering every status
- `ApplicationList` that takes `applications: readonly JobApplication[]` and renders one `ApplicationCard` per item
- An empty state ("No applications yet") when the array is empty

### Step by step
1. Write the sample data typed as `JobApplication[]`. Include at least one with `null` optional fields.
2. Write `ApplicationList` with `map` and `key={application.id}`.
3. Render a `<ul>` with each card inside an `<li>`.
4. Return the empty message early when the list is empty.
5. Render the list from `HomePage`, then pass `[]` to check the empty state.
6. Open the console and confirm there are no key warnings.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Keys use `id`, never the array index
- [ ] The empty state renders for `[]`
- [ ] Sample data type-checks with no casts
- [ ] Lint and build pass

### Hints
- An early `return` for the empty case keeps the main JSX flat.
- `readonly` in the prop type signals that the component will not change the list.
- `{count > 0 && ...}` can render `0`. Use a real boolean in conditions.

### Common mistakes
- Using `index` as the key, which breaks state when the list is filtered or reordered (Thursday).
- Putting the `key` on the inner card element instead of the outermost element returned by `map`.

### Stretch (optional)
- Sort the list by `appliedOn` descending without mutating the sample array.

### Check your understanding
- What does React use keys for, and what goes wrong with index keys?
- Why can `{list.length && <List />}` render a stray `0`?
- Where should the empty state live: in the list or in its parent?

days.learn: Value objects and equality; invariants in constructors
days.title: Value objects for email and URL fields with validation in the constructor
days.doneWhen: `EmailAddress` and `WebUrl` records reject invalid input in their constructors, two equal values compare `==`, and `dotnet test` is green with tests for both
days.brief:
### Why this matters
A `string` called `website` can hold anything. A `WebUrl` type can only hold a valid URL, so every method that receives one can trust it. Value objects are how you make invalid states impossible, and "entity vs value object" is a common design question.

### What you'll build
- `Common/EmailAddress` record with a single `Value`, validated in the constructor
- `Common/WebUrl` record that accepts only absolute `http` or `https` URLs
- `Company.Website` and `JobApplication.SourceUrl` switched from `string?` to `WebUrl?`
- A `RecruiterEmail` (`EmailAddress?`) on `JobApplication`
- Tests for valid, invalid and equality cases

### Step by step
1. Write `EmailAddress` as a `sealed record` with a constructor that trims, guards blank input and validates the format.
2. Write `WebUrl` the same way using `Uri.TryCreate` with `UriKind.Absolute` and a scheme check.
3. Throw a `DomainException` subclass (for example `InvalidValueException`) with the bad value in the message.
4. Change the entity properties to use the new types and fix the build.
5. Add a `Theory` per type with valid and invalid rows, plus one `Fact` that two equal values are `==`.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Invalid input cannot produce an instance
- [ ] Equality is by value, not reference
- [ ] Entities no longer take raw strings for these fields
- [ ] Tests cover valid, invalid and equality

### Hints
- Records give you value equality for free; you only add the invariant.
- `System.Net.Mail.MailAddress.TryCreate` is a reasonable email check. Perfect email validation does not exist; do not write a giant regex.
- Override `ToString()` to return `Value` so logs read well.

### Common mistakes
- Using a positional record without validation, so `new WebUrl("nope")` still works.
- Normalising in one place and comparing raw strings in another.

### Check your understanding
- What is the difference between an entity and a value object?
- Why validate in the constructor instead of in the endpoint?
- What does a record's `with` do to your invariant, and how could you protect it?

days.title: Status filter buttons that filter the list on the client
days.doneWhen: Clicking a status button shows only matching cards, "All" shows every card, and the filtered list is not stored in state

learnLinks.label: react.dev: Reacting to input with state

days.brief:
### Why this matters
State is where most React bugs come from. Learning to keep one small piece of state and compute everything else from it is the core of "thinking in React", and it is exactly what live coding rounds test.

### What you'll build
- An `ApplicationsView` that owns `status: ApplicationStatus | "All"` in `useState`
- A `StatusFilter` with one button per status plus "All", built from the `applicationStatuses` array
- The visible list computed during render with `filter`
- The active button marked with `aria-pressed`

### Step by step
1. Create `ApplicationsView` and move the list rendering from `HomePage` into it.
2. Add `useState<ApplicationStatus | "All">("All")`.
3. Write `StatusFilter` as a controlled component: it receives `value` and `onChange` as props and holds no state.
4. Loop over `["All", ...applicationStatuses]` to render the buttons.
5. Compute `visible` in the render body from the sample data and the filter.
6. Click every button and check the list and the empty state.

```tsx
const [status, setStatus] = useState<ApplicationStatus | "All">("All");
const visible = /* TODO: derive from sampleData and status */;
```

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Exactly one `useState`; the filtered list is not state
- [ ] `StatusFilter` is controlled and stateless
- [ ] The active button has `aria-pressed="true"`
- [ ] No TypeScript errors

### Hints
- If you can compute it from props or state, do not store it.
- Name callback props `onSomething` and handlers `handleSomething`.

### Common mistakes
- Keeping `filteredApplications` in state and syncing it with `useEffect`: two sources of truth.
- Typing `onChange` as `(value: string) => void`, which lets typos through.

### Stretch (optional)
- Add a text search on role title and combine both filters in the derived list.

### Check your understanding
- What is a controlled component?
- Why is the filtered list not state?
- What happens to the filter when `ApplicationsView` unmounts?

days.learn: Code coverage and what is worth testing
days.title: Coverage report with at least 80% on Domain
days.doneWhen: The HTML coverage report shows at least 80% line coverage on JobHunt.Domain

learnLinks.label: Microsoft Learn: Code coverage for unit testing
Microsoft Learn: Unit testing C# with xUnit

days.brief:
### Why this matters
Coverage tells you which lines never ran in a test. It does not tell you the tests are good. Knowing how to read a report, and deciding what is worth testing, is a senior habit and a common interview follow-up to "do you write tests?". This closes the .NET side of the PR "Domain model".

### What you'll build
- A coverage run with `dotnet test --collect:"XPlat Code Coverage"`
- An HTML report generated from the Cobertura XML (ReportGenerator is the usual tool, installed as a dotnet tool)
- New tests for the uncovered branches you decide matter
- A `coverage` script in the root `package.json`

### Step by step
1. Run the coverage command from `/api` and find the generated `coverage.cobertura.xml` under `TestResults`.
2. Install the report tool as a local or global dotnet tool and generate HTML into a `coverage-report` folder. Add that folder and `TestResults` to `.gitignore`.
3. Open the Domain project in the report and list every red line.
4. For each one decide: real behaviour (add a test), or dead code (delete it).
5. Re-run until Domain is at 80% or more.
6. Add the `coverage` script and mention it in the README.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Domain line coverage is 80% or higher
- [ ] Generated reports are ignored by Git
- [ ] No test was added that asserts nothing
- [ ] `npm run coverage` regenerates the report

### Hints
- The xUnit template already includes a coverage collector package; check the test `.csproj`.
- Branch coverage is stricter than line coverage. Look at it for your transition `switch`.
- Simple property getters rarely need their own test; they get covered by behaviour tests.

### Common mistakes
- Chasing 100% with tests that call code and assert nothing.
- Committing the `TestResults` folder.
- Counting the test project itself in the coverage numbers.

### Stretch (optional)
- Fail the run when coverage drops under 80% using the collector's threshold settings.

### Check your understanding
- What does 80% line coverage prove, and what does it not prove?
- What is the difference between line and branch coverage?
- Which code in JobHunt is not worth unit testing, and why?

days.learn: Derived state and lifting state up
days.title: Counts per status shown above the list, derived from the same state
days.doneWhen: Counts per status show above the list, change correctly with the sample data, and come from the same state as the filter with no extra `useState`; PR "Domain model" is merged
days.brief:
### Why this matters
Two components that need the same data must get it from a common parent. Deciding where state lives, and computing totals instead of storing them, is the "lifting state up" skill every React interview checks. Today also ends the week with the PR "Domain model".

### What you'll build
- A `StatusSummary` component showing counts like "Applied 3, Interviewing 2, Offer 1, Rejected 2"
- Counts derived from the full list in `ApplicationsView`, not stored
- Clicking a count selects that filter, so summary and filter share one piece of state
- "3 of 8 applications" text for the current filter

### Step by step
1. Write a pure function `countByStatus(apps): Record<ApplicationStatus, number>` in the feature folder.
2. Call it in `ApplicationsView` during render.
3. Build `StatusSummary` with props `counts`, `selected` and `onSelect`.
4. Pass the same `status` and `setStatus` (through a handler) to both the summary and the filter.
5. Add the "x of y" line.
6. Run `npm run lint`, `npm run build` and `dotnet test`, push the branch, open the PR "Domain model", review your own diff and merge.

### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Still exactly one `useState` in `ApplicationsView`
- [ ] `countByStatus` is a pure function with a typed return value
- [ ] Clicking a count and clicking a filter button stay in sync
- [ ] PR "Domain model" is merged with tests green

### Hints
- Start the counts object with every status at zero so the type is complete.
- `useMemo` is not needed for eight items. Measure before optimising.

### Common mistakes
- Keeping counts in state and updating them in an effect.
- Giving the summary its own selected state, so it drifts from the filter.
- Mutating the counts object inside `map` instead of using `reduce` or a plain loop on a fresh object.

### Check your understanding
- What does "lifting state up" mean, and when do you do it?
- What is derived state, and why is it safer than synced state?
- If the summary lived in the header, where would the state have to move?

days.title: From a blank file: a record, an enum, one guarded transition with a Theory test, and a typed React component that renders it
days.brief:
### The drill
From a blank file, write a record, an enum, one guarded transition with a `Theory` test, and a typed React component that renders the entity, in 30 minutes.

### Rules
- New empty folder outside the JobHunt repo; create projects with the CLI and `npm create vite`.
- Docs are allowed, but try without them first and write down every lookup. No AI assistants, no copying from JobHunt.
- Set a 30 minute timer: about 18 minutes on C# and 12 on React. Stop when it rings.

### Must include
- A class library and an xUnit project that references it
- A `record` value object in a new domain (for example `Money(decimal Amount, string Currency)`) that rejects bad input
- An enum with at least three states (for example `Pending`, `Paid`, `Shipped`)
- An entity with a private status setter, one guarded method and a custom exception
- One `[Theory]` with at least three rows covering legal and illegal moves
- A TypeScript union for the status and a component with typed props that renders the entity with a label from a `Record`

### Self-check
- [ ] Finished within 30 minutes
- [ ] `dotnet test` is green with zero nullable warnings
- [ ] The status changes only through the guarded method
- [ ] The Theory asserts the exception for an illegal move
- [ ] The component has no `any`
- [ ] You can explain why the value object is a record and the entity is not
- [ ] Lookup list written down

### If you got stuck
- Records, classes, nullable warnings: Monday, .NET part.
- The status union in TypeScript: Monday, React part.
- Guards and the domain exception: Tuesday, .NET part.
- Typed props and `Record` maps: Tuesday, React part.
- `Theory` syntax and test setup: Wednesday, .NET part.
- Value object validation: Thursday, .NET part.
